audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Wednesday, October twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six. The big thread today is the global reshuffling of international-student demand — and it runs straight through your higher-ed lane — so let's start there.

There are four signals landing at once this morning, and together they tell a coherent story. Start with the OECD. Their Education at a Glance twenty twenty-six report is out, and the headline finding is that international students are increasingly pursuing advanced degrees — graduate-level study, not just undergraduate pipelines — and that countries curbing international numbers through sweeping caps are taking a real economic hit. That matters because it reframes the entire recruitment conversation. For years the volume game has been about undergraduate headcount. The OECD data says the competitive frontier is moving up the value chain, toward master's and doctoral students who stay longer, pay more, and feed research and talent economies. For a Canadian institution trying to figure out how to grow net revenue in a capped environment, that's the strategic pivot — segment toward graduate-tier value propositions rather than fighting a losing volume war. That's a thought-leadership piece worth writing: reposition Canadian recruitment around the data, not around nostalgia for the old intake numbers.

Now put that next to Australia. Over the past six months, Australia's appeal to prospective international students has plunged — and the cause is policy, not demand. A sudden July decision pushed the study-visa application fee above two thousand Australian dollars, and refusal rates for several source countries spiked. The result is a measurable drop in interest. Australia is the clearest cautionary parallel for Canada right now, because our governments are pulling similar levers — fees, caps, refusals — and the Australian experience shows how quickly perception turns. When a destination signals it doesn't want you, students route around it. And critically, the ones who route away first are often the strongest candidates, the ones with options.

The UK is tightening too — raising the financial thresholds international students must demonstrate — and here at home, Canada is moving ahead with an asylum clampdown that's drawing sharp criticism from advocates. I'm flagging the Canadian piece less for its specifics and more for what it adds to the picture: another layer of policy uncertainty stacked onto an already jittery market. For your clients, the practical takeaway is that the enrollment environment is now defined by volatility, not by any single rule. The institutions that win will be the ones that can model multiple policy scenarios and move their recruitment spend fast — which is exactly where a disciplined, data-literate advisory voice earns its keep. The macro is redistributing demand. Whoever reads the redistribution fastest captures the mandate.

On the AI front, the most useful item today isn't a shiny product launch — it's a short letter in JAMA, and it's sharper than its format suggests. The authors respond to a piece on advertising inside AI-powered clinical decision-support tools, and they land a line worth stealing: these 'free' AI tools, they say, are the modern version of the drug-company pens and sponsored lunches of the nineteen-nineties. In other words, advertising is quietly embedding itself inside the AI layer that professionals are now trained to trust. Sit with that for a second, because it generalizes well beyond medicine. The entire premise of your AI Search Readiness work is that AI answer layers — ChatGPT, Perplexity, AI Overviews — are becoming the interface between a person and a decision. If commercial influence can be embedded invisibly inside a clinical AI assistant, the same dynamic is coming for every vertical: the assistant becomes the ad, and nobody sees the label. That's a content lane for you — 'when the assistant is the ad' — aimed at marketers and at public-institution governance leads who need to audit for sponsored influence inside the AI tools they're adopting. The higher-ed and public-sector angle is especially live, because institutions are deploying AI chatbots and advising tools with almost no framework for detecting commercial capture. That's your governance lens, and this JAMA letter is the hook.

The second AI item is more reassuring, and it's a good reminder that not every alarm is a catastrophe. Axios is calling it 'Black October.' After AI tools uncovered critical flaws in some of the web's foundational code, the cybersecurity world braced for a wave of automated attacks. Millions of hacking attempts followed — but very few succeeded. The bugs turned out to be genuinely hard to weaponize, and the defensive patching that companies rushed through appears to have held. Researchers are comparing it to Y2K: a real risk, aggressively mitigated, that looked like an anticlimax precisely because the mitigation worked. The lesson for any organization adopting AI tooling is that preparation is invisible when it succeeds. It's the kind of story worth remembering the next time a client pushes back on investing in governance and safeguards that don't produce a visible return — the absence of disaster is the return.

Two marketing items from Brandweek and Adweek that are worth your attention for the practice. First, Mastercard's marketing lead, Cheryl Guerin, with a contrarian line: democratized marketing won't differentiate your brand. Her argument is that as tools and tactics get commoditized and everyone has access to the same AI-assisted production, sameness becomes the default. Real differentiation comes from editorial discipline — from choosing what not to do. And she reframes agility, too: you can't be an agile marketer if you say yes to everything. That resonates directly with how you're positioning your own consultancy. In an AI-saturated market where everyone can generate competent output instantly, the scarce, premium skill is judgment — knowing what to decline. That's a selling point, not just an observation.

Second, Fanta's global VP on staying culturally relevant by handing consumers the mic — giving communities a genuine voice without letting them dictate brand direction. The nuance there matters. It's not 'let the audience run the brand'; it's 'let the audience shape the conversation while the brand holds the wheel.' For your higher-ed and real-estate clients, both of whom are tempted by user-generated and community-driven content, that's the governing principle worth articulating: participation, bounded by strategy.

Two items on the real-estate side, both structural rather than market-noise. The bigger one: OneKey MLS has joined the CRMLS lawsuit against Compass. The amended federal complaint asks a judge to affirm that public listing-cooperation rules comply with antitrust law — which is the crux of the fight over who controls listings, and whether a large brokerage can build walled gardens of private, pre-market inventory. This is a US case, but the principle reaches north. The tension between open cooperation and brokerage-owned private listing networks is a live question for any brokerage thinking about data strategy and inventory control. It's exactly the kind of industry structural shift worth tracking for the real-estate lane, because the outcome shapes what brokerages can and can't do with their listing data.

The second item is a California court ruling that cities can face damages for dragging out housing permits — the court found that permit seekers are the intended beneficiaries of a sixty-day ministerial duty on accessory dwelling units. Again, a US precedent, but the theme — courts putting teeth behind approval timelines — is one to watch as Western Canadian jurisdictions wrestle with how fast housing gets approved. Permit velocity is quietly becoming a legal and competitive issue, not just an administrative one.

Close to home now. Sun Peaks has tripled its stored summer snow ahead of the November ski-season opening — a hedge against a warm, uncertain early season. It's a small operational story, but it tells you the resort economy you live in is ramping hard into winter, and it's a reminder that snow reliability is now something the resort actively engineers rather than simply hopes for. Worth noting for the rhythm of the season and anything tied to the local short-term-rental market as visitors start arriving.

In Kamloops, Thompson Rivers University is signalling it wants to work constructively with the incoming B.C. Conservative government after the landslide win we discussed last week. This connects to the TRU enrolment story from Monday — domestic online enrolment is up while international numbers keep falling — so the institution is navigating both a funding-and-policy reset and a structural enrolment shift at the same time. For anyone watching the Canadian higher-ed market, TRU is a useful bellwether for how mid-sized public institutions adapt when the international tap tightens and the provincial government changes hands simultaneously.

And a safety note: Kamloops RCMP have charged a man after an unprovoked assault and robbery in the downtown core. Nothing systemic, but the kind of street-safety item worth being aware of if you or family are regularly downtown.

Two from the wider world. First, a tragedy in central Spain — a high-speed train slammed into the rear of a stopped train in Toledo province, derailing cars and killing at least thirty people. It's one of Spain's deadliest rail disasters in years, and investigators will be focused on how a train was allowed to approach a stopped one at speed.

Second, and more strategically relevant, Ukraine's Starlink disruptions are pushing Europe to look for non-Musk satellite alternatives. Restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink service temporarily disrupted drone operations, and that episode has rattled officials on both sides of the Atlantic. Rival firms like Eutelsat are now racing to loosen Elon Musk's grip on battlefield connectivity. The through-line here is one you can apply far beyond defence: single-vendor dependency is a systemic risk, and when one company controls critical infrastructure, its commercial or political whims become everyone's problem. That's a lesson that translates directly to how institutions think about dependence on a single AI provider — the same concentration risk, in a different domain.

Two health items, both from STAT. The first is a genuine development in the GLP-1 race: Eli Lilly reports that its triple-agonist drug, retatrutide — the so-called 'triple-G' — beat Novo Nordisk's Ozempic in a head-to-head diabetes study. Data keep accumulating that retatrutide becomes one of Lilly's biggest growth drivers. For you this sits in the category of 'know where the metabolic-health field is heading,' because these drugs are reshaping not just medicine but consumer behaviour and marketing across food, wellness and retail.

The second is a thoughtful pediatrician's opinion piece on managing families through measles anxiety — describing the dizzying reality of one family clamouring for the MMR vaccine while the family in the next room refuses it entirely. As case counts rise, it's a grounded, practical read on vaccine communication, and relevant for anyone with family health decisions in the mix.

One update to close the news. The MAID story from Monday has developed. Those who had sought medical assistance in dying for mental illness are describing the government's move to bar that access as 'a stab in the back.' The legislation restricting MAID in cases of mental illness is advancing, and the human response is now sharpening into organized backlash. It's a difficult, consequential policy debate playing out nationally, and worth following as it moves through Parliament.

That's your Wednesday, Midya. If you do one thing with this briefing, let it be the international-student thread — the OECD graduate-competition data paired with Australia's slide is a ready-made point of view, and it's precisely the kind of strategic reframing your higher-ed clients need right now. Keep the JAMA 'assistant as advertisement' idea in your back pocket too; it's a governance piece waiting to be written. I'll keep tracking the TRU and MAID stories as they develop. Talk tomorrow.
